source.title: BadLabel: A Robust Perspective on Evaluating and Enhancing Label-Noise Learning
source.authors: Jing-Feng Zhang; Bo Song; Hao-Han Wang; Bo Han; Tong-Liang Liu; Lei Liu; Masashi Sugiyama

record.file_problem: The full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports that DNNs fit noisy labels before clean labels under its BadLabel setting, qualifying the real-label-first claim in V6.
record.gate_note: The paper studies adversarially selected label noise, not completely random labels. Its test-accuracy tables do not report training error or test error at chance for random labels, so they do not bear on V1–V5. The row records the reported ordering of clean and noisy label losses before label perturbation.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own clean-versus-noisy loss comparisons and explicitly argues that early learning reverses under BadLabel, bearing on V6. Adversarial corruption defines the tested data condition; the networks are not explicitly trained to reverse the learning order.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately captures the local early-learning conclusion: BadLabel can reverse the early clean-versus-noisy loss ordering and subsequently make the distributions difficult to distinguish, undermining conventional loss-based selection. The paper's broader conclusion is that BadLabel degrades existing label-noise-learning methods and Robust DivideMix improves robustness under this corruption while remaining competitive under conventional noise.
record.recipe_differences: The paper crafts adversarially selected BadLabel corruption and studies loss ordering during noisy-label learning, rather than testing random labelings and training error.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported ordering is specific to BadLabel; after adversarial label perturbation, noisy-label losses become larger.
record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
record.problems: The evidence concerns adversarially selected BadLabel on CIFAR-10 rather than completely random labels. The loss-ordering result is illustrated at a single stated epoch and no uncertainty is reported for it.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 1–9 report test accuracy for noisy-label-learning methods under BadLabel and other noise types, not the random-label fitting or learning-order outcomes named by V1–V6. Figure 2(b) measures losses after an adversarial label perturbation and does not show the uninduced learning order.

untested.parts: Complete random labeling, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged training settings.
Time required to fit random versus real labels and convergence speed across corruption fractions.
Training fit on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian inputs.
Perfect training fit throughout the corruption range and test-error progression from clean to completely random labels. Test-accuracy tables alone do not establish the combined claim.
Whether explicit regularization prevents random-label fitting and whether removing it harms clean-label generalization.
Complete learning trajectories through memorization, completely random labels, and generality of the reported loss ordering beyond the illustrated settings.

missing.what: Clean-versus-noisy loss distributions under symmetric and instance-dependent corruption show the conventional clean-low-loss ordering. Record these conditions separately.
missing.locator: Section 3.5; Figure 1(b–c), bottom row; Appendix D specifies CIFAR-10, 40% noise, DivideMix, epoch 10.

missing.what: The later BadLabel comparison reports nearly indistinguishable clean and noisy loss distributions, complementing the reversed ordering at epoch 5.
missing.locator: Section 3.5; Figure 1(d), bottom row; Appendix D specifies CIFAR-10, 40% noise, DivideMix, epoch 10.

record.verdict_notes: BadLabel is adversarially selected corruption, not random labeling. The V6 verdicts concern qualitative loss-order evidence and the authors' interpretation; the figures do not establish complete memorization times. Figure 2(b) and the method-performance tables are already declared in rows_left_out.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labels, training error, chance test error, and unchanged architecture or hyperparameters.
Training time to fit random labels and convergence speed as corruption rises.
Perfect training fit and test-error progression across random-label corruption levels.
Whether regularization prevents fitting random labels or whether removing it harms true-label generalization.
The paper studies 40% adversarially generated BadLabel noise on CIFAR-10; it does not test completely random labels or establish a general training trajectory across settings.

rows.subject: DNNs
rows.operation_detail: Compared loss values for clean and noisy labels before adversarial label perturbation.
rows.measure: Relative loss values for noisy versus clean labels
rows.baseline: Clean labels had higher loss values than noisy labels.
rows.value: Noisy labels tend to have lower loss values.
rows.note: The authors interpret the loss ordering as DNNs fitting noisy labels first in this BadLabel setting.
rows.check: The qualitative loss ordering is correctly extracted. The baseline should identify clean-label losses as the comparator rather than repeat the result. This is an early-epoch loss comparison, not a measured time to complete memorization; no numerical separation or uncertainty is reported.
